content-type="pmc-pdf" xlink:href="jkms-25-1784.pdf"/><abstract><p>Antibiotic-associated diarrhea (AAD) is a common complication of antibiotic use. There is growing interest in probiotics for the treatment of AAD and <italic toggle="yes">Clostridium difficile</italic> infection because of the wide availability of probiotics. The aim of this multicenter, randomized, placebo-controlled, double-blind trial was to assess the efficacy of probiotic <italic toggle="yes">Lactobacillus</italic> (Lacidofil® cap) for the prevention of AAD in adults. From September 2008 to November 2009, a total of 214 patients with respiratory tract infection who had begun receiving antibiotics were randomized to receive <italic toggle="yes">Lactobacillus</italic> (Lacidofil® cap) or placebo for 14 days. Patients recorded bowel frequency and stool consistency daily for 14 days. The primary outcome was the proportion of patients who developed AAD within 14 days of enrollment. AAD developed in 4 (3.9%) of 103 patients in the <italic toggle="yes">Lactobacillus</italic> group and in 8 (7.2%) of 111 patients in the placebo group (<italic toggle="yes">P</italic>=0.44). However, the <italic toggle="yes">Lactobacillus</italic> group showed lower change in bowel frequency and consistency (50/103, 48.5%) than the placebo group (35/111, 31.5%) (<italic toggle="yes">P</italic>=0.01). Although the Lacidofil® cap does not reduce the rate of occurrence of AAD in adult patients with respiratory tract infection who have taken antibiotics, the <italic toggle="yes">Lactobacillus</italic> group maintains their bowel habits to a greater extent than the placebo group.</p></abstract><kwd-group><kwd>Probiotics</kwd><kwd><italic toggle="yes">Lactobacillus</italic></kwd><kwd>Antibiotic-associated Diarrhea</kwd></kwd-group><custom-meta-group><custom-meta><meta-name>pmc-status-qastatus</meta-name><meta-value>0</meta-value></custom-meta><custom-meta><meta-name>pmc-status-live</meta-name><meta-value>yes</meta-value></custom-meta><custom-meta><meta-name>pmc-status-embargo</meta-name><meta-value>no</meta-value></custom-meta><custom-meta><meta-name>pmc-status-released</meta-name><meta-value>yes</meta-value></custom-meta><custom-meta><meta-name>pmc-prop-open-access</meta-name><meta-value>yes</meta-value></custom-meta><custom-meta><meta-name>pmc-prop-olf</meta-name><meta-value>no</meta-value></custom-meta><custom-meta><meta-name>pmc-prop-manuscript</meta-name><meta-value>no</meta-value></custom-meta><custom-meta><meta-name>pmc-prop-legally-suppressed</meta-name><meta-value>no</meta-value></custom-meta><custom-meta><meta-name>pmc-prop-has-pdf</meta-name><meta-value>yes</meta-value></custom-meta><custom-meta><meta-name>pmc-prop-has-supplement</meta-name><meta-value>no</meta-value></custom-meta><custom-meta><meta-name>pmc-prop-pdf-only</meta-name><meta-value>no</meta-value></custom-meta><custom-meta><meta-name>pmc-prop-suppress-copyright</meta-name><meta-value>no</meta-value></custom-meta><custom-meta><meta-name>pmc-prop-is-real-version</meta-name><meta-value>no</meta-value></custom-meta><custom-meta><meta-name>pmc-prop-is-scanned-article</meta-name><meta-value>no</meta-value></custom-meta><custom-meta><meta-name>pmc-prop-preprint</meta-name><meta-value>no</meta-value></custom-meta><custom-meta><meta-name>pmc-prop-in-epmc</meta-name><meta-value>yes</meta-value></custom-meta><custom-meta><meta-name>pmc-license-ref</meta-name><meta-value>CC BY-NC</meta-value></custom-meta></custom-meta-group></article-meta></front><body><sec sec-type="intro"><title>INTRODUCTION</title><p>Antibiotic-associated diarrhea (AAD) is emerging as a common complication of antibiotic use. The frequency of AAD can be high (26-60%) during hospital outbreaks or intermediate (13-29%) during endemic periods and is relatively low in outpatient settings (usually less than 0.1%) (<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="B1">1</xref>, <xref ref-type="bibr" rid="B2">2</xref>). Risk factors for AAD include the use of broad-spectrum antibiotics, various host factors (old age, poor general condition), a longer hospitalization period and exposure to nosocomial pathogens (<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="B1">1</xref>-<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="B3">3</xref>). AAD can occur 2 to 8 weeks after exposure to antibiotics as a result of disruption of intestinal microflora. One of the main roles of normal gut microflora is to protect against colonization by intestinal pathogens (<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="B4">4</xref>). Once this protective barrier is broken, patients are more susceptible to infection with opportunistic pathogens. Probiotics have been proposed to treat AAD and <italic toggle="yes">Clostridium difficile</italic> disease. Probiotics mainly assist in re-establishing the disrupted intestinal microflora, enhancing immune responses and clearing pathogens and their toxins from the host (<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="B5">5</xref>-<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="B7">7</xref>).</p><p>There is growing interest in probiotics for the treatment of AAD and <italic toggle="yes">C. difficile</italic> disease because of the wide availability of probiotics as dietary supplements and concern over recent outbreaks of severe <italic toggle="yes">C. difficile</italic> disease in Canada and the United Kingdom (<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="B8">8</xref>, <xref ref-type="bibr" rid="B9">9</xref>). Research on probiotics has been reported for the past 28 yr (1977-2005), but the studies have been variable in trial design, type of probiotic and dosage and duration of treatment, and thus have often yielded contradictory results (<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="B10">10</xref>). Twenty-five randomized, controlled trials (RCTs) provided adequate data regarding the efficacy of probiotics for the prevention of AAD (<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="B10">10</xref>). Of the 25 RCTs, only 6 utilized <italic toggle="yes">Lactobacillus rhamnosus</italic> (<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="B11">11</xref>-<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="B16">16</xref>).</p><p>There were a few RCTs that proved the efficacy of <italic toggle="yes">Lactobacillus</italic> in preventing AAD, and debate arose regarding the study populations. A study on the use of <italic toggle="yes">L. rhamnosus</italic> (2×10<sup>10</sup> colonforming units per day) for preventing AAD in 302 adults receiving antibiotics at the Mayo Clinic showed no efficacy of <italic toggle="yes">L. rhamnosus</italic> in decreasing the overall incidence of AAD because quite a few patients had stool cultures, additional tests for diarrhea, or a positive diagnosis of <italic toggle="yes">C. difficile</italic> (<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="B15">15</xref>). However, 89 patients in a recent RCT on the daily administration of a <italic toggle="yes">Lactobacillus</italic>fermented milk product showed that it was safe and effective in the prevention of AAD (<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="B17">17</xref>). A recent RCT involving 135 patients demonstrated that a probiotic <italic toggle="yes">Lactobacillus</italic> preparation prevented AAD and <italic toggle="yes">C. difficile</italic>-associated diarrhea (<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="B18">18</xref>).</p><p>Therefore, we conducted a multicenter, randomized, placebo-controlled, double-blind trial to assess the efficacy of probiotic <italic toggle="yes">Lactobacillus</italic> (Lacidofil® cap) for the prevention of AAD in Korean adults.</p></sec><sec sec-type="materials|methods"><title>MATERIALS AND METHODS</title><sec><title>Participants</title><p>Adult patients receiving antibiotic therapy for respiratory tract infection were screened at 10 tertiary hospitals. The inclusion criteria were adult inpatients aged &gt;18 yr who received oral or injected antibiotics for respiratory tract infections within 48 hr of enrollment. The following patients were excluded from the study: 1) those who were diagnosed with <italic toggle="yes">C. difficile</italic> colitis within the previous 3 months, 2) those who were given tube feeding or who underwent an ileostomy or colostomy, 3) those with basal diarrheal disease (acute enteritis, inflammatory bowel disease, radiation enteritis, ischemic colitis and diarrhea caused by carcinoid), 4) those receiving other probiotics during the previous 15 days, 5) those treated with immunosuppressant drugs and those with immune deficiency, 6) those who underwent radiotherapy or chemotherapy treatment for cancer, 7) those treated with antidiarrheal, antispasmodic or motility agents for other diseases, 8) pregnant or lactating women, 9) those who underwent gastrointestinal surgery 3 months prior to the study, 10) those with a history of hypersensitivity to cephalosporins, penicillin or clavulanic acid, 11) those with verified diabetic autonomic neuropathy, 12) those who underwent organ transplantations, and 13) those with underlying conditions or diseases who, in the opinion of the investigator, were unsuitable for inclusion.</p></sec><sec><title>Study design</title><p>Between September 2008 and November 2009, a total of 214 patients with respiratory tract infection who had begun to receive antibiotics were randomly allocated to receive <italic toggle="yes">Lactobacillus</italic> (Lacidofil® cap) or a placebo for 14 days. This study was conducted at 10 investigational centers. Participants recorded their bowel frequency and stool consistency every day for 14 days. The primary outcome (AAD-1) was defined as loose or watery stools more than 3 times per day for at least 2 days within 14 days of enrollment. The secondary outcome (AAD-2) was defined as loose or watery stools more than 2 times per day for at least 2 days within 14 days of enrollment.</p><p>The admitting medical team identified eligible patients who had an antibiotic prescription for the treatment of respiratory tract infection. After the investigators obtained informed consent, they collected baseline data and prescribed the study drug on a randomized basis. The hospital pharmacy dispensed the drug. The treatment group received a probiotic preparation (Lacidofil® cap) containing <italic toggle="yes">L. rhamnosus</italic> R0011·<italic toggle="yes">L. acidophilus</italic> R0052 bacterial culture (2×10<sup>9</sup> colony-forming units), maltodextrin, Mg stearate, and ascorbic acid. The control group received a placebo drug composed of maltodextrin, Mg stearate and ascorbic acid. Participants began using the Lacidofil® cap or placebo drug within 48 hr of initiation of antibiotic therapy. The Lacidofil® cap and placebo were administrated at a dose of 1 capsule twice a day for 14 days. The administration of other drugs for accompanying diseases permitted subject to the investigator's judgment. The use of antidiarrheal (e.g., loperamide, polypcarbophil), antispasmodic (e.g., tiropramide, pinaverium, buscopan) or motility agents (e.g., domperidone, mosapride, itopride, levosulpride) that could affect the symptoms was prohibited. These drugs were withheld until the patient developed AAD, after which their use was allowed.</p><p>Investigators followed up participants for 14 days to check stool frequency, stool consistency and compliance. If participants had AAD, investigators collected further data on clinical symptoms and blood test results. As the safety of Lacidofil® cap has already been proven, its safety was not evaluated in this study.</p></sec><sec><title>Sample size</title><p>We estimated that the minimum sample size was 220 for each group. The sample size was calculated on the basis of an 18% difference in the proportion of AAD compared with the control group with an expected compliance rate of 80%, a statistical power (two sided) of 90%, a significance level of 5% and a dropout rate of 10%.</p></sec><sec><title>Randomization and double blinding</title><p>Among patients with respiratory tract infection, those who met the inclusion criteria were selected and allocated trial numbers. The subjects were allocated to the treatment (Lacidofil® cap treatment) or control groups (placebo) according to their trial numbers. To maintain double-blinding, the envelope containing the random trial number allocation code was sealed by the investigators, and the treatment allocations were not disclosed until the clinical trial was completed, except for cases for which access to the code was necessary. All investigators, participants, outcome assessors and data analysts were blinded throughout the study.</p></sec><sec><title>Statistical analysis</title><p>SPSS for Windows software (V. 13.0, SPSS, Chicago, IL, USA) was used for statistical analysis. The chi-square test was used to determine the difference in the incidence of AAD between the 2 groups, and the Student's t-test was used for analysis of continuous variables. Multiple logistic regression analysis was used to identify the risk factors for AAD, and effect estimates are presented as the odds ratio (OR) and 95% confidence interval (CI). For all analyses, a <italic toggle="yes">P</italic> value of 0.05 or less (two sided) was considered significant.</p></sec><sec><title>Ethics statement</title><p>The Institutional Review Board (IRB) of each hospital approved the study protocol (Ewha Womans University Mokdong Hospital, IRB No. 187-17). Written informed consent was obtained from each patient.</p></sec></sec><sec sec-type="results"><title>RESULTS</title><sec><title>Participant flow and baseline characteristics of participants</title><p>Patient flow is summarized in <xref ref-type="fig" rid="F1">Fig. 1</xref>. Over the 14-month study period, 286 patients were screened as potential candidates for this study by nurses. Of the 286 patients screened, 18 met 1 or more of the exclusion criteria, 28 did not meet all of the inclusion criteria, and 26 refused to participate in the study. Of the 214 patients who met the inclusion criteria and agreed to participate in the study, 42 failed to complete the study. Finally, 172 patients completed the study. Of the 42 patients who failed to complete the study, 5 had adverse events, 12 received contraindicated drugs, 21 did not continue the treatment protocol, and 4 were lost to follow-up. We performed intention-to-treat (ITT) analysis of data from 214 patients and per-protocol (PP) analysis of data from 172 patients.</p><p>Baseline characteristics are summarized in <xref ref-type="table" rid="T1">Table 1</xref>. The placebo (n=111) and the <italic toggle="yes">Lactobacillus</italic> groups (n=103) were similar in terms of their demographics and medical profiles at enrollment. There were no significant differences in total dose of antibiotics, baseline bowel movement, drug compliance, or pulmonary infections between the 2 groups. Respiratory tract infections, in descending order of frequency, were pneumonia, pulmonary tuberculosis, bronchitis, bronchiectasis, pleural effusion and upper respiratory tract infection.</p><p>Antibiotic use for both groups is summarized in <xref ref-type="table" rid="T2">Table 2</xref>. The antibiotics used were, in descending order, cephalosporin, macrolides, fluoroquniolones, antituberculosis drugs, clindamycin and penicillin. β-lactam antibiotics, including cephalosporins and penicillin, were commonly used in both the placebo and the <italic toggle="yes">Lactobacillus</italic> groups (75.7% vs 78.6%) (<italic toggle="yes">P</italic>=0.72). There were no significant differences in antibiotic use between the 2 groups.</p></sec><sec><title>Analysis of outcome measures</title><p>In ITT analysis (n=214), AAD-1 developed in 4 (3.9%) of 103 patients in the <italic toggle="yes">Lactobacillus</italic> group and in 8 (7.2%) of 111 patients in the placebo group (<italic toggle="yes">P</italic>=0.44). AAD-2 developed in 9 (8.7%) of 103 patients in the <italic toggle="yes">Lactobacillus</italic> group and in 16 (14.4%) of 111 patients in the placebo group (<italic toggle="yes">P</italic>=0.28). There was no significant difference in AAD occurrence between the 2 groups. However, no changes in bowel frequency or consistency were reported by 50 (48.5%) of 103 patients in the <italic toggle="yes">Lactobacillus</italic> group and by 35 (31.5%) of 111 patients in the placebo group (<italic toggle="yes">P</italic>=0.01). Increased bowel frequency over a period of more than 3 days during the 14-day period was observed in 47 (42.3%) of 111 patients in the placebo group and 31 (30.1%) of 103 patients in the <italic toggle="yes">Lactobacillus</italic> group (<italic toggle="yes">P</italic>=0.08) (<xref ref-type="table" rid="T3">Table 3</xref>). The results of multivariate analysis of the OR of <italic toggle="yes">Lactobacillus</italic> for AAD-1, AAD-2, and change in bowel frequency and consistency are shown in <xref ref-type="table" rid="T4">Table 4</xref>. The <italic toggle="yes">Lactobacillus</italic> group was less likely to experience changes in bowel frequency and consistency compared with the placebo group (OR 0.43, 95% CI 0.25-0.82), which means that although Lacidofil® cap does not reduce the rate of occurrence rate of AAD in adult patients with respiratory tract infection who have taken antibiotics, the <italic toggle="yes">Lactobacillus</italic> group maintained their bowel habits to a greater extent than the placebo group.</p><p>In PP analysis (n=172, excluding 42 patients who dropped out), AAD-1 developed in 3 (3.6%) of 83 patients in the <italic toggle="yes">Lactobacillus</italic> group and in 5 (5.6%) of 89 patients in the placebo group (<italic toggle="yes">P</italic>=0.72). AAD-2 developed in 8 (9.6%) of 103 patients in the <italic toggle="yes">Lactobacillus</italic> group and in 9 (10.1%) of 89 patients in the placebo group (<italic toggle="yes">P</italic>=1.00). However, normal bowel movement was reported by 36 (43.4%) of 83 patients in the <italic toggle="yes">Lactobacillus</italic> group and 27 (30.3%) of 89 patients in the placebo group (<italic toggle="yes">P</italic>=0.10) (<xref ref-type="table" rid="T5">Table 5</xref>). The results of multivariate analysis of the OR of <italic toggle="yes">Lactobacillus</italic> for AAD-1, AAD-2, and change in bowel frequency and consistency are shown in <xref ref-type="table" rid="T6">Table 6</xref>. The OR for no change in bowel frequency and consistency was 0.53 (95% CI 0.27-1.05, <italic toggle="yes">P</italic>=0.07).</p></sec><sec><title>Risk factors for AAD</title><p>The results of ITT analysis (n=214) of risk factors for AAD-1 (n=12) and non-AAD-1 (n=202) are shown in <xref ref-type="table" rid="T7">Table 7</xref>. AAD-1 was more prevalent in patients with no medical illness (75.0% vs 40.6%) (<italic toggle="yes">P</italic>=0.04) and those with a longer duration of antibiotic use (13.8±2.0 vs 11.9±3.6 days) (<italic toggle="yes">P</italic>=0.01). There was also a tendency for AAD-1 patients to have greater baseline bowel movement (1.4±0.7 vs 1.0±0.4 per day) (<italic toggle="yes">P</italic>=0.08), remnant drugs (9.2±11.4 vs 3.6±7.5 capsules) (<italic toggle="yes">P</italic>=0.06) or to use β-lactam antibiotics (100% vs 75.7%) (<italic toggle="yes">P</italic>=0.07). AAD-2 was more prevalent in patients who were younger (53±16 vs 62 ±15 yr) (<italic toggle="yes">P</italic>=0.01), had no medical illness (68.0% vs 39.2%) (<italic toggle="yes">P</italic>=0.01) or had a longer duration of antibiotic use (13.5±1.8 vs 11.8±3.7 days) (<italic toggle="yes">P</italic>=0.01). In addition, patients who developed AAD-2 had a tendency to have greater baseline bowel movement (1.3±0.6 vs 1.0±0.4 per day) (<italic toggle="yes">P</italic>=0.05), remnant drugs (5.8±8.8 vs 3.7±7.7 capsules) (<italic toggle="yes">P</italic>=0.07), or to use β-lactam antibiotics (92.0% vs 75.1%) (<italic toggle="yes">P</italic>=0.10).</p><p>The results of PP analysis (n=172) of the risk factors for AAD-1 (n=8) and non-AAD-1 (n=164) are shown in <xref ref-type="table" rid="T8">Table 8</xref>. AAD-1 tended to occur in patients who were younger (50±19 vs 60±16 yr) (<italic toggle="yes">P</italic>=0.06), or had elevated baseline bowel movement (1.4±0.5 vs 1.0±0.4 per day) (<italic toggle="yes">P</italic>=0.05). AAD-2 was more prevalent in patients who were young (51±16 vs 61±16 yr) (<italic toggle="yes">P</italic>=0.01), had a medical illness (23.5% vs 58.7%) (<italic toggle="yes">P</italic>=0.01), had a longer duration of antibiotic use (13.6±1.9 vs 12.3±3.4 days) (<italic toggle="yes">P</italic>=0.02) or use β-lactam antibiotics (100% vs 78.1%) (<italic toggle="yes">P</italic>=0.02). In addition, patients with AAD-2 had a tendency to have an increased baseline bowel movement (1.3±0.5 vs 1.0±0.4 per day) (<italic toggle="yes">P</italic>=0.06).</p></sec><sec><title>Adverse events</title><p>Mild abdominal discomfort was reported by 1 patient (0.9%) in the placebo group and by 3 patients (2.9%) in the <italic toggle="yes">Lactobacillus</italic> group (<italic toggle="yes">P</italic>=0.35). Skin eruption was reported by 1 patient (0.97%) in the <italic toggle="yes">Lactobacillus</italic> group. However, there were no significant adverse events associated with the use of Lacidofil® cap.</p></sec></sec><sec sec-type="discussion"><title>DISCUSSION</title><p>This study evaluated the efficacy of a <italic toggle="yes">Lactobacillus</italic> probiotic single-agent regimen for AAD. In our study, the number of AAD cases was not statistically different between the 2 groups and the prevalence of AAD was low (3.9-7.2%) compared with a previous report (2-25%) as assessed by ITT analysis (<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="B2">2</xref>). This result may be attributed to the short-term follow-up period because AAD may occur up to 2 months after stopping antibiotic treatment (<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="B1">1</xref>). Recent meta-analysis of 10 randomized, blinded, placebo-controlled trials showed that the combined risk ratio (RR) of developing AAD was significantly lower in the <italic toggle="yes">Lactobacillus</italic> groups than in the placebo group (RR 0.35, 95% CI 0.19-0.67) (<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="B19">19</xref>). Large differences exist among trials, including our study. The indications for antibiotic therapy differed among the studies and included respiratory tract infection, otitis media, urinary tract infection and <italic toggle="yes">Helicobacter pylori</italic> infection (<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="B19">19</xref>).</p><p>According to a previous report, doses used in <italic toggle="yes">Lactobacillus</italic> regimens range from 2×10<sup>9</sup> to 4×10<sup>10</sup> colony-forming units per day (<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="B19">19</xref>). There was considerable variation in the probiotic regimens used. It has been suggested that doses of probiotics should exceed 10<sup>10</sup> colony-forming units per day (<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="B10">10</xref>). In our study, the dose of the <italic toggle="yes">Lactobacillus</italic> regimen was 4×10<sup>9</sup> colony-forming units. This may be the reason why the <italic toggle="yes">Lactobacillus</italic> group preparation did not exhibit a protective effect for AAD. Thus, it is expected that if the does had been greater (&gt;10<sup>10</sup> colony-forming units per day), it may have had a preventive effect on AAD. The effects of increasing dosages of probiotics should be monitored, irrespective of whether adverse events are expected. Further evaluations using standardized <italic toggle="yes">Lactobacillus</italic> dosage forms and regimens are warranted.</p><p>AAD was defined as loose or watery stools more than 3 times per day for at least 2 days. This stringent definition enabled us to differentiate between clinically relevant and clinically unimportant changes in the consistency of stools. The secondary outcome, AAD-2, was defined as loose or watery stools more than 2 times per day for at least 2 days. However, definitions of AAD vary between published studies. For example, Vanderhoof et al. defined diarrhea as ≥2 liquid stools per 24 hr on ≥2 days (<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="B13">13</xref>). Bowel frequency and consistency reflects bowel habits. Tables 3 and 4 showed that there were significant differences in bowel frequency and consistency. These results suggest that maintenance of usual bowel habit was promoted by the probiotic. This result is consistent with that of a previous trial (<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="B20">20</xref>) performed on children. Although the overall incidence of diarrhea was surprisingly low and the administration of a combination of <italic toggle="yes">Bifidobacterium longum</italic> PL03, <italic toggle="yes">L. rhamnosus</italic> KL53A, and <italic toggle="yes">L. plantarum</italic> PL02 did not significantly alter the incidence of diarrhea, it reduced the daily frequency of stools (<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="B20">20</xref>).</p><p>In our study, ITT (n=214) analysis gave better results than PP (n=172) analysis. Forty-two patients did not complete the study. Thus, the number of patients enrolled was less than that required to achieve the target statistical power for the PP analysis. Studies involving larger numbers of patients are necessary. Regarding risk factors, patients who had elevated baseline bowel movements, more remnant drugs, and greater use of β-lactam antibiotics had higher incidences of AAD-1 and AAD-2. These results show that patients with elevated bowel movement and low drug compliance had a higher incidence of AAD. However, increased bowel movements may have affected the underlying risk for development of AAD or their response to the probiotic. Thus, for analysis of the OR of <italic toggle="yes">Lactobacillus</italic> (<xref ref-type="table" rid="T4">Tables 4</xref>, <xref ref-type="table" rid="T6">6</xref>), we adjusted the data for baseline bowel movement and other confounding factors (age, medical illness, duration of total antibiotic use, and remnant drugs). β-lactam antibiotics, including penicillin and cephalosporins, are proven risk factors for AAD (<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="B1">1</xref>). In addition, AAD was more prevalent in subjects who were young, had no medical illness and had used antibiotics for a long period. Our result is not in accord with that of a previous report (<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="B1">1</xref>). The reason for this may be selection bias in our study.</p><p><italic toggle="yes">L. rhamnosus</italic> has inhibitory activity against a wide range of bacteria, including <italic toggle="yes">C. difficile</italic> (<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="B21">21</xref>). In addition, <italic toggle="yes">L. rhamnosus</italic> is expected to be useful for the prevention of AAD because it survives the digestive process and is not killed by the acidic pH of the stomach or by bile (<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="B22">22</xref>). When administered exogenously, <italic toggle="yes">L. rhamnosus</italic> persists in the colon for at least a week and modifies the colonic environment with potential positive health effects (<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="B23">23</xref>, <xref ref-type="bibr" rid="B24">24</xref>). There are 3 reports showing <italic toggle="yes">L. rhamnosus</italic> prevents AAD in children (<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="B12">12</xref>-<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="B14">14</xref>). For adults, 2 reports have been published concerning the synergistic effect of <italic toggle="yes">L. rhamnosus</italic> with anti-<italic toggle="yes">H. pylori</italic> eradication therapy (<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="B11">11</xref>, <xref ref-type="bibr" rid="B16">16</xref>). The rationale for the use of probiotics is that the use of antibiotics may result in a disturbance of the normal intestinal microflora, which is one of the key factors in the pathogenesis of AAD and <italic toggle="yes">C. difficile</italic> infection (<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="B25">25</xref>). There are several possible mechanisms by which probiotics, including <italic toggle="yes">Lactobacillus</italic>, exert preventative effects on AAD. These include the synthesis of antimicrobial substances (<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="B17">17</xref>, <xref ref-type="bibr" rid="B22">22</xref>, <xref ref-type="bibr" rid="B26">26</xref>), competition for nutrients required for the growth of pathogens, competitive inhibition of adhesion of pathogens, and modification of toxins or toxin receptors (<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="B27">27</xref>).</p><p>Concerns about the safety of probiotics have been raised because probiotics are living organisms that, when given to ill patients, could elicit adverse reactions. As some intestinal bacteria have been shown to migrate from the intestine to other organs, antibiotic-resistant gene acquisition is also a potential concern (<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="B10">10</xref>). Although bacteremia and fungemia have been reported in the literatures (<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="B28">28</xref>, <xref ref-type="bibr" rid="B29">29</xref>), our study showed only mild abdominal discomfort in 1 patient and skin eruption in 3 patients without any significant adverse events. Caution should be exercised for patients who are severely ill and are receiving nutrition or antibiotics through a potentially open portal catheter or a nasogastric tube.</p><p>Our study had some limitations. First, the incidence of AAD was much lower in our study than in previous studies. Our patients were followed up for only 2 weeks after antibiotic therapy. As AAD can occur up to 2 months after stopping antibiotic treatment (<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="B1">1</xref>), some cases might have been missed. Second, the patients were not normally distributed. Some centers recruited more patients than allocated, and others had fewer cases. This imbalance was caused by differences in the hospital size and location, and the incidence of antibiotic-naïve respiratory infections at the hospitals. Third, the difference between hospitals in the main antibiotic prescribed is a potential weakness because the incidence of AAD differs between groups of antibiotics. However, there was no significant difference in antibiotic use between the 2 groups. Finally, although the required sample size was 220, we performed the study using 214 patients. The most frequent limitation of previous studies may also have been insufficient power to detect significant differences (<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="B19">19</xref>). Few investigators have calculated required sample sizes, and 3 investigators reported that slow recruitment of study patients resulted in premature termination of the trial (<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="B10">10</xref>, <xref ref-type="bibr" rid="B30">30</xref>). However, our study has value as the first prospective, randomized, double-blind, multicenter study on the effect of probiotic <italic toggle="yes">Lactobacillus</italic> for the prevention of AAD in Korea.</p><p>In conclusion, although Lacidofil® cap does not reduce the occurrence of AAD in adult patients with respiratory tract infection who have taken antibiotics, the <italic toggle="yes">Lactobacillus</italic> group maintains their bowel habits to a greater extent than the placebo group without any significant adverse events.</p></sec></body><back><fn-group><fn fn-type="supported-by"><p>This study was supported by the research fund of the Korean Association for the Study of Intestinal Diseases. There was no conflict of interest between the Lacidofil® cap pharmaceutical company (Pharmbio Korea Co., Ltd.) and this study.</p></fn></fn-group><ref-list><ref id="B1"><label>1</label><element-citation publication-type="journal"><person-group person-group-type="author"><name name-style="western"><surname>McFarland</surname><given-names>LV</given-names></name></person-group><article-title>Epidemiology, risk factors and treatments for antibiotic-associated diarrhea</article-title><source>Dig Dis</source><year>1998</year><volume>16</volume><fpage>292</fpage><lpage>307</lpage><pub-id pub-id-type="pmid">9892789</pub-id><pub-id pub-id-type="doi" assigning-authority="pmc">10.1159/000016879</pub-id></element-citation></ref><ref id="B2"><label>2</label><element-citation publication-type="journal"><person-group person-group-type="author"><name name-style="western"><surname>Bartlett</surname><given-names>JG</given-names></name></person-group><article-title>Clinical practice.
